paragraphs: Generating a molecule’s three-dimensional structure can require many successive updates, making generation speed a practical bottleneck. This paper investigates the sequence of intermediate states produced during generation to understand where that work goes. Its central finding is that geometric graph generators must establish an ordering of the molecule’s atoms before refining their atomic feature values.

The authors use this diagnosis to divide generation into a permutation phase and an adjustment phase. This distinction gives the acceleration method two specific targets: resolving atom ordering and refining the resulting representation. They introduce a geometry-informed prior and a consistency parameter objective to accelerate these phases, connecting the design of the method to the observed structure of the generation process.

Experiments report competitive performance with approximately ten sampling steps. The method is about 7.5 times faster than previous state-of-the-art models and about 100 times faster than diffusion-based models in the reported comparisons. The contribution is therefore both a diagnosis of the generation trajectory and an acceleration approach built around that diagnosis.
neurips-2025-accelerating-3d-molecule-ge.tldr: Diagnosing molecule generation as atom ordering followed by feature refinement enables competitive generation in approximately ten sampling steps.

paragraphs: AI research agents can automate the design, implementation, and training of machine learning models, but their success depends on how they explore possible solutions. This paper studies that exploration on MLE-bench, where agents tackle real-world machine learning problems drawn from Kaggle competitions. It treats an agent as a search policy operating over candidate solutions.

In this formulation, operators are the actions used to modify a candidate, while the search policy determines how exploration proceeds. The authors systematically vary both operator sets and search strategies, including greedy search, Monte Carlo tree search, and evolutionary search. Their findings emphasize the interaction between these choices: the available modifications and the strategy for choosing among candidates jointly shape performance.

The best combination raises the rate of achieving a Kaggle medal on MLE-bench lite from 39.6% to 47.7%, reported as a state-of-the-art result. This supports designing research agents around coordinated search and modification mechanisms. The paper also highlights evaluation methodology as part of understanding and advancing automated machine learning.
neurips-2025-ai-research-agents-for-mach.tldr: Jointly designing research agents’ search strategies and solution-modification operators improves medal success on MLE-bench lite.

paragraphs: Models that predict the effects of biological mutations are commonly compared using scores averaged over benchmark datasets. Those averages provide limited insight into how performance relates to the structure of the underlying sequence-fitness landscape: the relationship between biological sequences and their measured fitness. This paper adds landscape information to make such comparisons more informative.

The authors introduce GraphFLA, a Python framework for constructing and analyzing fitness landscapes across DNA, RNA, proteins, and other modalities. It accommodates datasets containing millions of mutants and computes twenty biologically relevant features covering four fundamental aspects of landscape topography. These features provide descriptions of the prediction setting alongside the usual measures of model accuracy.

Applying GraphFLA to more than 5,300 landscapes from ProteinGym, RNAGym, and CIS-BP helps the authors interpret results from dozens of prediction models and identify their respective advantages. They also release 155 combinatorially complete empirical landscapes containing over 2.2 million sequences. Together, the framework and datasets support comparisons that connect model performance to characteristics of the biological landscapes being predicted.
neurips-2025-augmenting-biological-fitne.tldr: GraphFLA adds fitness-landscape characteristics to biological benchmarks, helping explain differences in mutation-prediction performance.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can represent several plausible action sequences or trajectories, making them useful for planning and control. A separate challenge is ensuring that generated plans satisfy constraints. Constrained Diffusers addresses this by incorporating constraints on the generated distribution into pretrained diffusion models, without requiring retraining or changes to their architecture.

The method modifies the reverse diffusion process using constrained Langevin sampling. It combines trajectory optimization with constraint satisfaction through three iterative approaches: projection, primal-dual optimization, and augmented Lagrangian methods. This places constraint handling inside the process that produces the plan, allowing the sampling procedure to account for both the desired trajectory and its admissibility.

For online control, the framework adds discrete control barrier functions to provide safety guarantees within its formulation. It repeatedly generates a short plan, executes its first action, and replans. Experiments in Maze2D, locomotion, and PyBullet ball-running tasks report constraint satisfaction with lower computation time and competitive performance against existing methods, including settings with static constraints and constraints that change over time.
neurips-2025-constrained-diffusers-for-s.tldr: Constrained Diffusers adds constraint-aware sampling and online safety mechanisms to pretrained diffusion planners without retraining.

paragraphs: A model can look easy to interpret while still giving misleading impressions of which inputs carry information about its target. This paper examines suppressor variables: non-informative features that can receive false-positive importance attributions. The problem affects both explanations applied after training and direct interpretations of linear models and generalized additive models.

The authors generalize activation patterns, an approach originally developed for interpreting linear models, to the broader family of additive models. The resulting method, PatternGAM, uses univariate generative surrogate models to distinguish target-related information from suppression effects involving nonlinear features. They also introduce PatternQLR for polynomial models. The aim is to correct feature importance rather than assume that an additive structure makes its interpretation reliable.

Evaluations on XAI-TRIS use a new false-negative-invariant version of an earth mover’s distance accuracy metric and show significant improvements over popular attribution methods and conventional additive-model interpretation. Case studies on COMPAS and MIMIC-IV further illustrate how separating genuine information from suppression changes the interpretation of particular features.
neurips-2025-correcting-misinterpretatio.tldr: PatternGAM and PatternQLR correct misleading feature importance caused by suppressor variables in additive and polynomial models.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets clients collaborate, but differences between their data can make shared knowledge unreliable. This paper identifies two problems with using knowledge distillation to address those differences. Directly matching a global model through forward Kullback–Leibler divergence can introduce substantial bias when its outputs have multiple peaks. Meanwhile, conflicting updates from different domains can make the global teacher inaccurate in particular domains.

DKDR addresses the matching problem by dynamically balancing forward and reverse Kullback–Leibler divergence according to discrepancies in knowledge. This changes how clients fit the teacher’s outputs instead of relying on one fixed direction of comparison. To address the teacher’s reliability, the framework also decouples knowledge to identify domain experts from which clients can obtain more reliable domain-specific information.

The two components target different weaknesses: the route by which knowledge is transferred and the source supplying that knowledge. Experiments on single-domain and multi-domain image classification support the effectiveness of DKDR and the efficiency of its key modules. The findings connect reliable distillation with both adaptive output matching and domain-sensitive teacher selection.
neurips-2025-dkdr-dynamic-knowledge-dist.tldr: DKDR improves federated distillation by adapting its distribution-matching objective and drawing domain knowledge from identified experts.

paragraphs: Reference-driven image completion fills missing regions in a target image using other views. Large viewpoint differences make this difficult because visually plausible content can still be geometrically misaligned. GeoComplete introduces explicit three-dimensional structural guidance so that completion can account for how the scene should appear from the target viewpoint.

Its diffusion architecture has two branches. One generates the missing image regions from the masked target, while the other extracts geometric features from a projected point cloud. Joint self-attention lets the branches exchange information during completion. This couples image synthesis with a geometric representation, giving the generator structural cues beyond those available from image appearance alone.

GeoComplete also projects the target view into reference images to identify occluded regions and masks those areas during training. This target-aware masking directs learning toward reference cues useful for the target view. Experiments report a 17.1% improvement in PSNR over state-of-the-art methods, together with improved geometric accuracy and high visual quality. The results support combining explicit geometry with selective use of reference information.
neurips-2025-geocomplete-geometry-aware-.tldr: GeoComplete combines projected 3D geometry and target-aware reference masking to improve image completion across differing viewpoints.

paragraphs: Scientific generative models often need to evaluate how likely their generated samples are. For applications such as Boltzmann Generators, these likelihood calculations can become prohibitively expensive as the system grows. HollowFlow targets this bottleneck with a flow-based model designed to make likelihood evaluation scale more favorably.

The method uses a non-backtracking graph neural network to enforce a block-diagonal Jacobian, a structured arrangement of the model’s derivatives. This allows likelihood evaluation with a number of backward passes that stays constant as system size increases, yielding theoretical speed-ups of up to quadratic order in system size. The constant-pass claim concerns the number of backward passes, rather than stating that all computation takes constant time.

The authors also show how any equivariant graph neural network or attention-based architecture can be adapted to their non-backtracking framework. Tests train Boltzmann Generators on two systems of increasing size, with sampling and likelihood-evaluation improvements following the predicted scaling. A hundredfold speed-up on the larger system demonstrates the practical potential of the proposed derivative structure.
neurips-2025-hollowflow-efficient-sample.tldr: HollowFlow structures model derivatives to accelerate scientific sampling and likelihood evaluation, reporting a hundredfold speed-up on its larger test system.

paragraphs: Neural network optimizers must turn gradient information into parameter updates, and that information carries uncertainty. KOALA++ explicitly models structured gradient uncertainty using a Kalman-based optimization approach. Its goal is to capture useful relationships in uncertainty while keeping the computation practical for large training problems.

The method estimates parameter covariance by recursively updating compact gradient covariance products. This extends the original KOALA framework, which assumed diagonal covariance and therefore used a more restricted uncertainty representation. KOALA++ captures richer structure implicitly, avoiding storage of the full covariance matrix and large matrix inversions. It also avoids the expensive second-order gradient calculations used by second-order optimization methods.

Experiments across tasks including image classification and language modeling report accuracy matching or exceeding state-of-the-art second-order optimizers, while retaining the efficiency associated with first-order methods. The contribution is a way to make structured uncertainty useful without explicitly maintaining its full matrix representation. The reported results support that trade-off across the tested tasks, linking the compact recursive representation to both competitive accuracy and computational efficiency.
neurips-2025-koala-efficient-kalman-base.tldr: KOALA++ captures structured gradient uncertainty through compact covariance products, achieving competitive optimization without full covariance storage.

paragraphs: This paper studies sampling from discrete distributions whose probabilities are known only up to a normalizing constant. The target assigns relative probability through an energy function, but the overall normalization is unavailable. Such problems arise in statistical physics, machine learning, and combinatorial optimization, and become especially challenging when there are many possible states and several distinct regions of high probability.

Masked Diffusion Neural Sampler, or MDNS, learns a neural sampling process by aligning two path measures. Here, the comparison concerns distributions over sampling trajectories, rather than only their final states. A family of learning objectives carries out this alignment, with its theoretical foundation supplied by stochastic optimal control of continuous-time Markov chains.

Experiments cover distributions with different statistical properties and extremely high dimensions. The authors report accurate sampling, strong efficiency and scalability, and large improvements over other learning-based baselines. Ablations and extensions further examine the framework’s components and potential. These findings support trajectory-distribution alignment as a practical training principle for difficult discrete sampling problems.
neurips-2025-mdns-masked-diffusion-neura.tldr: MDNS learns to sample difficult discrete distributions by aligning sampling-path distributions using objectives grounded in stochastic optimal control.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation can benefit from depth or thermal inputs alongside RGB images, but processing each modality through a separate backbone adds substantial cost. MixPrompt introduces auxiliary information into a pretrained RGB segmentation model through a lightweight prompting module. The existing RGB backbone keeps its architecture and remains frozen during training.

The prompting module starts from early layers of a pretrained RGB feature extractor. At each backbone layer, it aligns RGB and auxiliary features across multiple low-rank subspaces, providing compact channels for combining their information. An additional mixing scheme enables interaction between those subspaces. Training updates only this module and the segmentation head, concentrating adaptation in a relatively small portion of the system.

Across NYU Depth V2, SUN-RGBD, MFNet, and DELIVER, MixPrompt improves mIoU over two-branch baselines by 4.3, 1.1, 0.4, and 1.1, respectively, while using nearly half the parameters. It also outperforms recent prompting methods at similar compute budgets. These results show that auxiliary modalities can provide useful segmentation gains through compact adaptation of a frozen RGB model.
neurips-2025-mixprompt-efficient-mixed-p.tldr: MixPrompt adds depth or thermal information to a frozen RGB segmentation backbone with lightweight prompts, improving accuracy with fewer parameters.

paragraphs: Studying ancient manuscripts requires substantial expert time, and the usefulness of large multimodal models for this work has received limited evaluation. MS-Bench creates a structured test grounded in a Dunhuang case study. Developed with archaeologists, it contains 5,076 high-resolution images dating from the fourth through fourteenth centuries and 9,982 expert-curated questions.

The questions cover nine subtasks aligned with archaeological workflows. The authors evaluate thirty-two models using four prompting strategies, examining effectiveness, robustness, and cultural contextualization. This connects model assessment to the kinds of judgments involved in manuscript study, while also testing how the presentation of a task affects a model’s response.

The analysis finds that greater model scale improves performance and reliability in the evaluation. Chain-of-thought prompting has mixed effects, whereas prompts augmented with visual retrieval provide consistent benefits. Which tasks suit a model also depends on its visual capabilities. Current models cannot replace domain expertise, but the findings indicate potential for future human–AI collaboration that accelerates manuscript research.
neurips-2025-ms-bench-evaluating-lmms-in.tldr: MS-Bench evaluates multimodal models on expert-designed manuscript tasks, finding useful potential alongside a continuing need for domain expertise.

paragraphs: Turning a natural-language optimization problem into a working program requires accurate interpretation, a valid mathematical formulation, and verification of the result. MURKA organizes this process around three specialized agents: an Extractor, a Solver, and a Checker. The framework combines reinforcement learning and knowledge distillation to align their contributions.

The Extractor uses group relative policy optimization with rewards covering semantic correctness and execution fidelity. The Solver learns from a stronger teacher model through distillation, producing structurally valid, executable formulations in AMPL. The Checker then uses feedback from the optimization solver to iteratively verify solution correctness. This division assigns understanding, formulation, and checking their own explicit roles.

Built on LLaMa3-8B, MURKA is evaluated on eight operations-research benchmarks, including NLP4LP, ComplexOR, and NL4Opt. The reported results show a 5.9 percentage-point absolute improvement in solution accuracy and a 5.1% increase in execution success rate over leading baselines. These findings support the framework’s robustness across the tested problem domains and its potential for practical optimization applications.
neurips-2025-murka-multi-reward-reinforc.tldr: MURKA coordinates trained extraction, formulation, and checking agents to improve the accuracy and executability of optimization programs.

paragraphs: Automatically creating three-dimensional bounding boxes can reduce annotation costs in autonomous driving and support recognition of previously unseen objects. Existing approaches often treat objects uniformly and refine annotations through repeated self-training. OpenBox addresses these issues with a two-stage pipeline that uses a two-dimensional vision foundation model and accounts for objects’ physical states.

The first stage associates instance-level cues extracted from images with corresponding three-dimensional point clouds. Context-aware refinement improves this association between image evidence and spatial data. The second stage categorizes instances according to rigidity and motion state, then generates adaptive bounding boxes using class-specific size statistics. These distinctions let the annotation process respond to differences between the objects it encounters.

OpenBox produces its annotations without self-training, removing the need for repeated annotation-refinement cycles of that kind. Experiments on the Waymo Open Dataset, Lyft Level 5 Perception, and nuScenes report improvements in accuracy and efficiency over baselines. The results support combining foundation-model image cues with physical-state-aware box generation for automatic 3D annotation.
neurips-2025-openbox-annotate-any-boundi.tldr: OpenBox creates 3D bounding-box annotations by connecting image cues to point clouds and adapting boxes to object rigidity and motion.

paragraphs: Layout-to-image generation asks a model to produce an image from an arrangement of object bounding boxes. This paper examines a difficult case: layouts in which those boxes overlap heavily. It identifies two sources of difficulty, large overlapping regions and overlapping objects with little semantic distinction, and demonstrates their effects through qualitative examples and quantitative analysis.

To measure the difficulty of these layouts, the authors introduce OverLayScore, which quantifies bounding-box overlap complexity. They find that existing benchmarks favor simpler layouts with low scores. OverLayBench addresses that imbalance with high-quality annotations and a balanced distribution of OverLayScore values, making demanding overlap cases a more deliberate part of evaluation.

The paper also proposes CreatiLayout-AM, trained on a curated amodal mask dataset, as an initial approach to improving generation under complex overlaps. Its contributions connect a diagnosed failure mode with a metric, a benchmark, and a model direction. This gives researchers a more focused basis for assessing progress on crowded layouts where conventional evaluations provide limited coverage.
neurips-2025-overlaybench-a-benchmark-fo.tldr: OverLayBench and OverLayScore make dense object overlap a systematic test of layout-to-image generation.

paragraphs: PartCrafter generates multiple meaningful three-dimensional mesh parts from a single RGB image. It handles individual objects and multi-object scenes within one generation architecture, without requiring the image to be segmented first. The result is a structured collection of geometrically distinct parts, making decomposition part of the generation process itself.

The model builds on a pretrained whole-object mesh diffusion transformer, reusing its weights, encoder, and decoder. Each part receives its own set of disentangled latent tokens, and all parts are denoised simultaneously. Hierarchical attention connects information within each part and across the collection. This structure supports detailed individual components while coordinating their contribution to a coherent overall result.

The authors curate part-level supervision by mining annotations from large 3D object datasets. Experiments report better generation of decomposable meshes than existing approaches, including parts that are not directly visible in the input image. These findings support the value of learned part-aware generative priors for producing structured 3D content from limited visual evidence. Code and training data are released.
neurips-2025-partcrafter-structured-3d-m.tldr: PartCrafter jointly generates distinct, coordinated 3D mesh parts from one image, including parts hidden from view.

paragraphs: Vision-language models have advanced the operation of digital interfaces, but physical appliance panels pose a less explored challenge. PUO-Bench provides annotated panel images paired with vision-language instructions to evaluate understanding and operation in these settings. It creates a task-specific resource for studying how models interpret controls encountered in the physical world.

Experiments reveal substantial performance differences between models used without task-specific training and models fine-tuned for panel understanding and operation. The authors interpret this gap as evidence that existing models lack important capabilities for these tasks. The benchmark therefore helps identify a practical capability gap that broader progress on digital interfaces does not resolve by itself.

The paper also introduces a privacy-preserving architecture that performs panel understanding on an edge device and sends complex reasoning to a cloud language model. Raw visual data stays off the cloud, reducing privacy risks associated with its transmission. The authors acknowledge a performance trade-off caused by edge-model limitations, making the framework an explicit balance between local visual processing and remote reasoning.
neurips-2025-puo-bench-a-panel-understan.tldr: PUO-Bench tests physical control-panel understanding, while an edge–cloud framework reduces privacy risks by keeping raw images local.

paragraphs: Low-Rank Adaptation reduces the cost of fine-tuning by learning compact matrix updates. That low-rank restriction can also reduce representational ability and lead to weaker performance. RidgeLoRA aims to preserve the lightweight character of LoRA while approximating the capabilities of full-rank training more closely.

The method combines a new architecture with a matrix-ridge-enhanced full-rank approximation. Its design avoids requiring high memory usage and large numbers of parameters simply to restore matrix rank. The authors also provide a mathematical derivation establishing a better upper bound on representations than standard LoRA. This theoretical result addresses the representation limitation that motivates the architecture, alongside the empirical investigation of its practical behavior.

Across experiments in multiple domains, RidgeLoRA performs better than other LoRA variants and can match or surpass full-rank training. These are reported experimental outcomes, rather than a claim that every adaptation task will favor RidgeLoRA. The findings indicate that a lightweight adaptation architecture can recover substantial representational flexibility while retaining the efficiency motivation behind low-rank fine-tuning.
neurips-2025-ridgelora-matrix-ridge-enha.tldr: RidgeLoRA adds a matrix-ridge-enhanced approximation to lightweight adaptation, with experiments showing performance that can rival full-rank training.

paragraphs: This paper studies how attention capacity depends on the number of attention heads and the hidden dimension within each head. The authors observe that increasing head count improves multi-head attention performance when the hidden size per head remains sufficiently large. That condition motivates a method for expanding both aspects while keeping the model compact.

Simulated Attention Score, or SAS, projects low-dimensional head representations into a higher-dimensional space to simulate additional heads and larger per-head representations without increasing parameter count. The authors extend the same simulation principle to the feature dimensions of key and query embeddings. A complementary mechanism, Parameter-Efficient Attention Aggregation, controls the parameter cost of combining attention information.

Experiments across multiple datasets and tasks report significant improvements over different attention variants. The central idea is to separate the size of the learned representation from the larger attention computation it can simulate. The reported findings support this approach as a way to improve expressiveness while preserving model size, grounded in the observed relationship between head count and per-head capacity.
neurips-2025-sas-simulated-attention-sco.tldr: SAS simulates more attention heads and larger feature dimensions through compact representations, improving attention performance without enlarging the model.

paragraphs: Producing large reasoning datasets is difficult when generated reasoning is uncontrolled, inconsistent, or repetitive. Caco uses executable code as the basis for synthesizing instruction and chain-of-thought training data. Its aim is to scale verified reasoning examples beyond approaches limited to predefined mathematical problems.

The process first fine-tunes a code-based reasoning generator on existing mathematical and programming solutions expressed in a unified code format. It then generates diverse reasoning traces and validates them through code execution and rule-based filtering. Filtered outputs are reverse-engineered into natural-language instructions and reasoning traces. This creates an automated loop connecting executable reasoning with language-based training examples, with executability guaranteed by the process.

Using the resulting Caco-1.3M dataset, trained models outperform strong existing baselines on mathematical reasoning benchmarks. Further analysis attributes better generalization to unseen tasks to code-anchored verification and instruction diversity. The contribution connects data scale with a concrete validation mechanism: generated reasoning is checked through execution before being converted into the language forms used for training.
neurips-2025-scaling-code-assisted-chain.tldr: Caco automatically generates reasoning training data by executing and filtering code traces, then converting them into natural-language tasks and explanations.

paragraphs: Larger neural networks can perform worse in deep reinforcement learning, making scale difficult to use reliably. This paper investigates the causes of that behavior through empirical analyses. The findings suggest that non-stationarity interacts with gradient pathologies arising from suboptimal architectural choices, contributing to the difficulty of increasing network size.

The authors respond with direct interventions that stabilize gradient flow during learning. Their approach links the proposed fixes to the diagnosed training behavior, rather than treating network size alone as the problem. The interventions are described as simple to implement and compatible with established reinforcement learning algorithms, allowing the stabilization strategy to be used within familiar training setups.

Evaluation across different agents and environment suites shows robust performance over a range of network depths and widths, including strong results at large scales. The causal interpretation remains grounded in empirical evidence: the analyses suggest an explanation, and the interventions test its usefulness. Together, the findings support gradient stability as an actionable factor in making larger reinforcement learning networks train effectively.
neurips-2025-stable-gradients-for-stable.tldr: Empirical analyses link reinforcement-learning scaling difficulties to unstable gradients, and simple stabilization interventions improve performance across network sizes.

paragraphs: Video diffusion transformers are costly to run, and quantization offers a way to reduce their memory and computation requirements. This paper identifies a particular obstacle: modeling space and time together produces extremely long token sequences, making calibration sensitive to data selection and creating learning difficulties. S²Q-VDiT addresses both issues within post-training quantization.

Its Hessian-aware Salient Data Selection method builds calibration datasets using characteristics of both video diffusion and quantization. The second component, Attention-guided Sparse Token Distillation, uses the model’s sparse attention patterns to emphasize tokens with greater influence on its output. Together, these mechanisms focus calibration on useful examples and distillation on influential parts of the long token sequences.

Under W4A6 quantization, using four-bit weights and six-bit activations, the authors report lossless performance with 3.9-fold model compression and 1.3-fold faster inference. Those results apply to the reported quantization setting. The approach shows how selecting calibration data and allocating learning attention across tokens can work together to preserve video-generation performance while reducing deployment cost.
neurips-2025-text-s-2-q-vdit-accurate-qu.tldr: S²Q-VDiT combines selective calibration data and attention-guided token distillation to compress video diffusion transformers while preserving reported performance.

paragraphs: Neural networks sometimes develop new behaviors abruptly during training, but the timing and mechanisms of these changes remain difficult to explain. This paper focuses on one specific phenomenon: the emergence of sparse attention in Transformers. Studying this concrete attention pattern provides a tractable setting for investigating how learning dynamics produce an apparently sudden change.

The authors combine theoretical analysis of a toy model with experiments on small Transformers trained on a variant of linear regression. They identify mechanisms behind sparse attention emergence and find that its timing follows power laws related to task structure, architecture, and optimizer choice. They also find that repetition can substantially accelerate the emergence of the pattern.

The results are additionally confirmed on an in-context associative recall task. The paper therefore offers a theoretically grounded account supported across these studied settings. Its scope is one form of emergence: how sparse attention develops. Within that scope, the findings connect the timing of learned structure to the data distribution, model design, and repetition during training.
neurips-2025-the-emergence-of-sparse-att.tldr: Theory and small-Transformer experiments explain sparse attention emergence, showing power-law timing and substantial acceleration from repetition.

paragraphs: Clustering fairness depends partly on how each data point’s loss is measured. In centroid clustering, loss reflects distance to a representative point. In non-centroid clustering, it reflects the largest distance to another point in the same cluster. This paper brings those previously separate settings together through semi-centroid clustering, where loss combines both measurements.

Within this unified setting, the authors study proportional fairness criteria inspired by proportional representation: the core and its weaker relaxation, fully justified representation. Their main result is a polynomial-time algorithm that achieves a constant-factor approximation to the core. The guarantee still applies when centroid and non-centroid losses use different distance metrics, allowing the two components to measure distance differently.

The paper also establishes improved results for restricted loss functions and for the weaker fairness criterion, together with lower bounds in each case. These results distinguish what can be guaranteed in the general framework from what becomes possible under narrower requirements. The contribution is a shared mathematical treatment of fairness across two clustering paradigms and their combination.
neurips-2025-unifying-proportional-fairn.tldr: Semi-centroid clustering unifies two loss definitions and admits a polynomial-time constant-factor approximation to core fairness.

paragraphs: Diagnosing language-model hallucinations is difficult because several underlying causes can interact. This paper proposes an account based on competing associations: more frequent associations that conflict with facts or context can outweigh faithful ones. The framework connects an incorrect output to the learned relationships that favor it, giving hallucination analysis a specific mechanism to investigate.

Through theoretical and empirical analysis, the authors argue that decoder-only Transformers effectively act as subsequence embedding models, with fully connected layers storing input-output associations. They then introduce a tracing algorithm that varies input contexts randomly and examines how hallucination probabilities change. The purpose is to identify causal subsequences associated with the model’s erroneous output.

Experiments show that the tracing method identifies hallucination causes better than standard attribution techniques, and evidence from the training corpus supports its findings. This links the proposed mechanism, the diagnostic procedure, and the data from which associations were learned. The contribution is a framework for understanding and tracing hallucination behavior through subsequence associations, supported by the paper’s theoretical and empirical analyses.
neurips-2025-why-and-how-llms-hallucinat.tldr: The paper explains hallucinations through competing learned subsequence associations and introduces a tracing method to identify their causes.
